bio.en: Ryan Hoover is the founder of Product Hunt and a full-time investor through his fund Weekend Fund, and previously spent time as a product manager before becoming a well-known figure in tech.
bio.zh: Ryan Hoover 是 Product Hunt 的创始人，也是通过其基金 Weekend Fund 全职从事投资的人，在成为科技圈知名人物之前，他曾担任过产品经理。

summary.en: Ryan reflects on the surreal experience of building Product Hunt into a tech institution and the hidden weight of public recognition, while openly discussing the anxiety and mask of confidence that come with being a founder/CEO. He shares lessons from his writing and investing, and the importance of community and showing up authentically. The conversation blends personal vulnerability with practical founder wisdom.
summary.zh: Ryan 回顾了将 Product Hunt 打造成科技圈标志性产品的超现实经历，以及公众知名度背后隐藏的重量，同时坦诚分享了身为创始人/CEO 伴随而来的焦虑与“自信面具”。他分享了写作与投资中的心得，以及社区与真诚在场的重要性。本期将个人的脆弱坦诚与务实的创始人智慧融为一体。

turns.speaker: Ryan
turns.en: I don't know how to articulate that- that feeling, but that flutter in your stomach that you wake up with in the morning of just anxiety and stress and- and worry. Um, being a CEO or founder makes it slightly harder, uh, in some ways, because you still have to put on this mask. You have to put on this space of confidence externally and- and internally as well, where people need to trust you. You also don't want to subject them to the same anxiety that you're feeling and be a 100% transparent.
turns.zh: 我不知道该如何形容那种感觉——那种早上醒来时胃里涌起的焦虑、压力和担忧。嗯，作为CEO或创始人，情况会稍微复杂一些，某种程度上是因为你仍然需要戴上这副面具。无论是外部还是内部，你都需要展现出自信的形象，让人们信任你。但你又不想让他们承受你所感受到的焦虑，所以必须保持百分之百的透明。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Ryan Hoover is the founder of Product Hunt, which you already know. He's also former product manager, which I did not know. Currently, he's a full-time investor with his fund, the Weekend Fund. He's also an author of a bunch of great block posts and an actual book, called Hooked. He's also really good on Twitter and in my opinion, a very special human being. Ryan Hoover, welcome to the podcast.
turns.zh: 瑞安·胡佛（Ryan Hoover）是Product Hunt的创始人，你们应该都认识他。不过我之前不知道他还曾担任过产品经理。目前，他是Weekend Fund基金的全职投资者，还是多篇精彩博文和《上瘾》（Hooked）一书的作者。他在推特上也非常活跃，在我看来，他是个非常特别的人。瑞安·胡佛，欢迎做客播客。

turns.speaker: Ryan
turns.en: Hey, Lenny. Thanks for having me. I've been reading a lot of your blog posts over, I don't know, past two or three years now, and I'm glad to- to see you do the podcast now. It's cool.
turns.zh: 嘿，莱尼（Lenny）。感谢邀请我。我过去两三年里读了你很多博文，很高兴现在看到你做播客了。太棒了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Thank you, man. That compliment will go straight to my heart. And I will think about it often. I appreciate that.
turns.zh: 谢谢兄弟。这番称赞我会铭记于心的，以后会经常回味。真的很感激。

turns.speaker: Ryan
turns.en: Cut- cut that and put it on Twitter. There you go. Yeah. [laughs]
turns.zh: 剪掉这段，放到推特上。好了。对。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: You're such a tech celebrity; everybody knows Product Hunt. Everybody knows Ryan Hoover, at least in tech. And I'm curious, how often are you recognized walking around the street, in life, and has there ever been like a super awkward or super hilarious moment of that?
turns.zh: 你简直是科技界的名人啊，每个人都知道Product Hunt。Ryan Hoover在科技圈可是家喻户晓的。我很好奇，在现实生活中走在街上时，有多少人认出你？有没有特别尴尬或搞笑的经历？

turns.speaker: Ryan
turns.en: Yeah, so t- Product Hunt started in late 2013 and quickly got a lot of traction in- in the tech- tech sphere. So, yeah, people in tech, um, might recognize me. People outside of tech, doubt- doubt they recognized me. Um, I actually do wonder subconsciously if I grew my hair out to avoid being recognized. Um, I'm not sure if it's true or not, but anyway, it's been a couple years or so growing my hair out and I'm like, ah, I just kinda wanna like disappear sometimes. But, you know, in San Francisco, where everybody's in tech, um, there was a lot of that. And probably the- the, the moment where I was like, "Oh, this is- this is like a thing," uh, it was probably early Product Hunt, uh, I was at- do you remember... I don't know if you know this. Do you know a club, um, called DNA Lounge, and they did something-
turns.zh: 是的，Product Hunt于2013年底上线，很快在科技圈引起了轰动。所以，科技圈的人可能认得我，但圈外的人应该不太会认出我。说实话，我甚至怀疑自己留长头发是为了避免被认出来。不知道是不是真的，但反正留了几年长发，有时真想消失不见。不过在旧金山这个科技圈大本营，确实经常被认出来。最让我意识到自己出名的一次，是Product Hunt刚起步时，我参加了DNA Lounge的Bootie派对——

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Mm-hmm.
turns.zh: 嗯。

turns.speaker: Ryan
turns.en: ... Called Bootie every Saturday-
turns.zh: ……每周六都是狂欢派对。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Mm-hmm.
turns.zh: 嗯。

turns.speaker: Ryan
turns.en: ... It was like a mash-up dance party.
turns.zh: ……融合了各种舞曲风格。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.speaker: Ryan
turns.en: Yeah. Super well known in the Bay Area. Really fun, fun, uh, kind of experience. Anyway, I remember being with friends and drinking, like- like one does and somebody turns around and says, “Is that the Product Hunt guy?”
turns.zh: 是啊。在湾区非常有名。真的很有趣，超好玩的。总之，我记得当时和朋友们喝着酒，像平常一样放松，突然有人转过头问：“那不是Product Hunt的家伙吗？”

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: [laughs]

turns.speaker: Ryan
turns.en: And that was the first time that sort of happened in that setting where I was like, oh gosh, now I have to like, think about my actions. And I can't just like, be entirely like loose and, you know, relax with my friends. And, um, so anyway, there- there's always pros and cons to those types of things. Um, but you know, it- it definitely is makes me more aware of, I'm already a very, like sometimes anxious and like self-aware person in terms of like my surroundings. And so when you combine that with, “Oh, these strangers might be watching me,” is not the best thing in the world, but it's okay.
turns.zh: 那是我第一次在这种场合被认出来，瞬间意识到自己的一举一动都被关注，不能再随心所欲地和朋友们放松了。总之，这种关注有利有弊。不过我已经很习惯时刻留意周围环境了，所以被陌生人注视的感觉其实还好。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I've actually gone a little bit through that same experience recently in my, like a much smaller sense where I- with this newsletter and the growth of this thing, there’s been like meetups happening all over the world. And so I've been going to the SF meetups here and there, and it feels very strange to be like, known and people get- they’re like taken pictures with me, like what the- what the hell's going on. ‘Cause I started this thing as, uh, COVID hit and it was like- everyone's at home, I was just typing on my computer, didn’t have to go anywhere. And as the world has emerged, it's become a new- a new thing I'm dealing with, on a much smaller scale.
turns.zh: 事实上，最近我也经历了类似的经历，虽然规模小得多。我通过这份时事通讯和它的发展，世界各地都开始举办见面会。我时不时会去旧金山的见面会，但被认出后那种感觉很奇怪——人们给我拍照，问我怎么回事。这让我很困惑，因为我是在新冠疫情爆发时创办这份时事通讯的，那时大家都宅在家，我只是在电脑前敲字，不需要到处跑。如今世界逐渐恢复正常，但这成了我需要面对的新挑战，只不过规模小得多。

turns.speaker: Ryan
turns.en: Yeah. Yeah. Events are events are fun. Um, we threw a bunch of them at- at Product Hunt. Uh, yeah, you- you do a lot of selfies and a lot of like, handshakes and it’s- there's, there's some energy there. I'm an introvert though. So by hour, like three or four, I'm just like, ugh… uh… I need to use the restroom cause I haven't been able to escape and I'm socially exhausted, so, but they are fun.
turns.zh: 是啊是啊。这类活动挺有趣的。我们在Product Hunt上办过很多。嗯，你会拍很多自拍，握很多手，现场气氛很热烈。不过我是个内向的人，所以到了三四点的时候，我就会想，哎呀……得去上厕所了，因为根本没法脱身，社交太累了。不过还是挺有意思的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I know, uh, exactly what you mean. I am also an introvert and I get so drained doing things like that. I was gonna ask you about that. So yeah. Um, along the same lines, you’re- you're a very public person. You tweet a lot, you share a lot, you do a lot of podcasts and things like that. What's something that people don't know about you?
turns.zh: 我懂的，我也是个内向的人，做这类事也会很疲惫。我正想问你这事呢。所以嗯，嗯。顺便说一句，你是个很高调的人。在推特上发很多东西，分享很多内容，还做很多播客之类的。但人们不知道的你的事情有哪些呢？

turns.speaker: Ryan
turns.en: Yeah. Um, you're right. I- I probably sh- maybe overshare, uh, on Twitter and other things…
turns.zh: 是啊。你说得对。我可能在推特上或者其他地方分享得太多了……

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: No, that, that is not what-
turns.zh: 不，不，不，不是那个意思——

turns.speaker: Ryan
turns.en: Um, there is a list of [laughs] no, no, I know. I know what you're saying. Um, but there's also a whole series of things that I don't talk about. Um, some of them- well, anyway, I won't, I won't talk about the things I can't talk about. Uh, but one thing that, um, one thing that most people don't know about- I know there- there's certain juicy things, uh, like everybody has in their life. Um, I recently moved to- well, I guess it's been a year. Um, I moved to Miami about a year ago and, uh, I haven't been talking about it publicly, primarily because I just didn't want to be lumped into, oh, another person moving to Miami. Like, I, I don't know. I just, there's no benefit or like, reason for me to do so. Uh, I want my friends there in Miami to know I'm there, but otherwise I don't need the world to know. I guess now they will. Um, that said in Miami, you know, we’re- we're there about two thirds of the year, so I'm actually in California right now. Um, as you know, the summer humidity come- comes through Miami and hurricane season. We’re- we're planning to do more of, um- I wouldn't call it nomadic and I wouldn't call it bicoastal per se, but something like that. Where two thirds of the year we’re Miami and then maybe a third were in New York, or LA, or someplace else. Um, and I love that. Um, fortunately we have the flexibility, uh, when I say we, my girlfriend, Susie, and I, to just carry our laptops and work anywhere. So it's been- it's been a nice lifestyle kinda shift.
turns.zh: 嗯，确实有不少事我不方便说……嗯，有些事——反正我不会谈那些不能公开的事。嗯，但有件事大多数人都不知道——我知道有些八卦消息，比如每个人生活里都有的那些趣事……嗯，我最近搬到迈阿密了，嗯，大概有一年了。嗯，我大约一年前搬到迈阿密的，但一直没公开，主要是不想被归为又一个“搬到迈阿密的人”。我也不知道，就是觉得没必要这么做。嗯，我想让迈阿密的朋友知道我在那儿，但其他人没必要知道。现在他们应该知道了。嗯，在迈阿密住的时间占全年大约三分之二，所以我现在在加州。嗯，你知道的，迈阿密的夏天湿度大，还有飓风季。我们计划多去一些地方……嗯，我不会说这是游牧生活，也不会说这是两地生活，但差不多就是这样。一年有三分之二在迈阿密，然后三分之一可能在纽约、洛杉矶或者其他地方。嗯，我很喜欢这种生活方式。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I did not know that, that is very interesting. Why did you get pulled into Miami? What pulls you there?
turns.zh: 我不知道这事儿，真有意思。你为什么搬到迈阿密？是什么吸引你去那儿的？

turns.speaker: Ryan
turns.en: Yeah. You know? Um, so the way I describe ci- cities are kinda like a product. So if you're in the supermarket or- supermarket, I sound like an, old- old person. Ha, if- if you're at a store, you're looking at different products, or if you're online, you're evaluating different products, and they each have like a cost and they have some benefits, um, or values or whatever you- you want to use to describe it. And for me, each city is kind of like that. And so, you know, in terms of costs, there's cost of living in terms of housing, uh, food, taxes, a bunch of things that go into the cost of living in the city. And then the city provides a lot of benefits and- and things like that. And so in LA- so I was in bay area for ten years, LA for two Miami for one. Now, they each have their own pros and cons. They each cost effectively different prices. And so we visited Miami a year and a half ago and we just fell in love with lot- lots of it. Um, we also- it's just cheaper. It's cheaper than the Bay Area. It's cheaper than LA. Um, when- when you kind of count, kinda like all in costs, um, and we had a bunch of friends move there, so we enjoyed the city. We're like, this is good., strong ROI. Uh, this is a good product. Let’s- let's move there. Um, but at the same time, as I mentioned, like- we are traveling and, and exploring other cities. So it’s- it's kind of the best of both worlds for us.
turns.zh: 是啊。你知道吗？嗯，我把城市比作产品。就好比你在超市里挑选商品——我听起来像个老古板。哈哈，如果你在商店里挑选不同产品，或者在网上评估不同产品，每样产品都有成本和优势，或者说价值之类的。对我来说，每个城市都类似于这样。就成本而言，城市生活成本包括住房、食物、税收等诸多方面。而城市也能提供诸多好处等等。比如我在湾区待了十年，洛杉矶待了两年，迈阿密待了一年。每个城市都有各自的优缺点，成本也各不相同。一年半前我们去过迈阿密，一下子就爱上了那里。嗯，那里生活成本更低，比湾区低，比洛杉矶也低。综合所有成本因素，我们还有很多朋友搬到了那里，所以我们很享受这座城市。我们觉得这很棒，投资回报率很高。这是个很棒的产品，让我们搬过去吧。不过正如我之前提到的，我们也会继续旅行探索其他城市。对我们来说，这真是两全其美。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Very cool. Um, curious how long you last there and how you like it over time. I love Miami. I always have a good time when I go there. And I have many friends living there. Changing topics, a little bit, something that I've noticed you do recently, which is super cool is you offer people the chance to DM you questions that they have about their startup or their journey as a founder. And you just offer to give 'em free advice. And then sometimes you, tweet the DMs to share that with more folks. I'm curious just how many people have DM’d you because this is such a cool offer, and what have you learned going through this and kind of hearing people's questions?
turns.zh: 太棒了。嗯，我很好奇你在那里待了多久，随着时间推移你对那里的感受如何。我很喜欢迈阿密，每次去那里都玩得很开心。还有很多朋友住在那里。换个话题，我最近注意到你有个很酷的做法，就是给人们提供机会，通过私信向你提问，关于他们的创业项目或创业历程。你主动提供免费建议，有时还会把这些私信分享给更多人。想知道有多少人私信过你，毕竟这真是个超棒的提议。通过这个过程，你学到了什么？

turns.speaker: Ryan
turns.en: I first opened up my DMs- I had 'em closed, which is like traditionally the default on Twitter for a long time. ‘Cause I was like, “Oh, if I open them up, I'll just get a bunch of spam and I don't need another inbox to- to call through.” I opened it up quietly and, um, actually didn't get a lot of spam, uh, surprisingly. Like yeah, people would shill something or promote something, but it wasn't too bad. So I- I left it open and then I forget, one day I was maybe I was like- on the elliptical, bike or the recumbent bike or something. And I was just… I- I tend to get on the bike and just hold my phone up and just do emails and work. And so, um, I just said, “Hey, DM me if you have any questions, any founders, and I'll try and like answer as many as I can.” And, um, part of my motivation for that was… I don't know, I was just killing time. And the other was, I used to blog a lot. I used to write a lot, um, I don't know, I've written hundreds of blog posts, but not so much anymore. I rarely write anymore. And part of it's because it just takes so long to write. And sometimes I don't feel like inspired by any topic. It’s- it's sort of like a writer's block. And so I found this also kind of as a means to like, do micro- almost like micro blog posts in a way, uh, where the prompt is the question from somebody else. I don't have to think about the pr- prompt. And then the answer is- is in some ways, a way for me to actually think about that- that topic, almost like refine my own thinking in, in some sense. And so I started doing that and then I realized, “Well, maybe other people have similar questions, and maybe other people have other answers and other ideas too,” so I would just take a screenshot of my answer and kind of summarize their answer, of course, keeping it anonymous, not sharing anything that would be sensitive. Um, and just put it on Twitter and- you know, it's been fun. I do that maybe once every three or four days, I share a new question and answer and, sort of like a… It's like micro blogging in a way, I guess that’s what Twitter is, but like it's a kind of like a real micro-blogging kind of like, uh, um, activity for me.
turns.zh: 我首先打开了私信功能——之前我一直把它关闭着，这在推特上其实是默认的设置。我当时想：“哦，如果我打开私信功能，肯定会收到一堆垃圾信息，我又不需要另一个收件箱来处理这些消息。”但出乎意料的是，我打开后并没有收到太多垃圾信息。虽然还是有人会推销产品或推广项目，但情况还不算太糟。所以我保持私信功能开启，然后有一天我忘了关闭，可能当时我在椭圆机上锻炼，或者骑着躺式自行车之类的。我习惯一边骑车一边处理邮件和工作。于是我发了一条消息：“如果有任何问题，或者想认识创业者的，可以私信我，我会尽可能回复。”这么做部分原因是想打发时间，还有就是我以前经常写博客，写了很多文章，但现在写得越来越少了。写作太耗时间了，有时又找不到灵感，就像写作障碍一样。所以我把这当作一种微型博客的形式，问题来自别人，答案由我自己构思。这样我既不必费心构思主题，又能借此深化自己的思考。后来我发现，其他人可能也有类似的问题，也会有不同的见解，于是我会截取他们的回答，并进行总结，同时保持匿名，不分享敏感信息。然后把这些内容分享到推特上，感觉挺有趣的。我大概每三四天分享一次问题，和回答，某种程度上这就像微型博客——毕竟推特本质上就是这样一种平台，对我来说就是一种实实在在的微型博客活动。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Is there anything that's kind of surprised you, or that you've learned from founders? What they ask you about? Like, “Wow, I didn't expect this was gonna be such a common problem or question.”
turns.zh: 有没有什么让你感到惊讶的，或者从创业者那里学到的东西？他们问你些什么？比如，“哇，我没想到这会是个如此常见的问题或难题。”

turns.speaker: Ryan
turns.en: I wouldn't say anything like super surprising. However, a lot of people… So, you could do the same thing on Twitter and say, “Hey, AMA, ask me anything in public,” the thing is people are not gonna ask certain things, um, for a lot of reasons. And maybe the biggest surprise was a lot of people are pretty vulnerable. These are strangers, founders who DM me saying, “Hey, I’m- we have three months runway left. We’re running out of money. Here's a situation. What advice do you have?” Or just things that, you know, everyone has to wear this unfortunate mask is kind of the way I- what I used to describe it. This mask in life, in business, where everything is going great. And you know, you're super confident, there are no problems. You got it all under control. And so the reality is that's not the case. Like [laughs] if you peered inside of almost every single company, it probably looks chaotic in- in different ways. And so I guess- I guess maybe the biggest surprise or thing that I value the most is the authenticity of people willing to share some of these, um, vulnerable moments and questions.
turns.zh: 我倒不会说这有多令人惊讶。不过，很多人……所以，你可以在推特上做同样的事，说“嘿，AMA，随便问我公开问题”，问题是人们不会问某些问题，原因有很多。最令人惊讶的或许是很多人其实很脆弱。这些都是陌生人，创始人私信我说：“嘿，我们只剩三个月的时间了。钱快花光了。这是个情况。你有什么建议？”或者就是那种，每个人都必须戴着这个不幸的面具——这就是我过去常描述的。这个面具存在于生活和商业中，看似一切顺利。你超级自信，没有问题。一切尽在掌控。但现实并非如此。比如[笑]如果你深入了解几乎每一家公司，它很可能在不同方面显得混乱。所以我猜——我猜最令人惊讶或最珍视的，是那些愿意分享这些脆弱时刻和问题的真诚之人。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. What's interesting about your format is as you were talking, I kind of realized it's very similar to my newsletter format, which I- which I think is part of the reason it worked is it's based on people asking me a question, and then I answer the question, and then-
turns.zh: 太棒了。你的格式很有趣，当你说话时，我突然意识到这和我的新闻通讯格式非常相似。我觉得这部分成功的原因之一是它基于人们向我提问，然后我回答问题，再然后——

turns.speaker: Ryan
turns.en: It's true.
turns.zh: 确实如此。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: … And that ends up forcing you to have like concrete, actionable advice. So you've kind of developed even more interesting way of doing it on Twitter, where it's more focused. So, very smart.
turns.zh: ……而这最终迫使你给出具体、可行的建议。所以你在推特上开发了更有趣的方式，更具针对性。太聪明了。

turns.speaker: Ryan
turns.en: I've always liked your format by the way, in that you are, um- you're a curator in many sense. Like- yeah, you have a lot of experience and good ideas, but you're not trying to answer all the questions in that you are really pulling in experts in their domain expertise to like find answers or inspiration. And I've always liked that format because one; it, I think leads to a better- better results, better content, better answers, but also it's arguably easier. Um, like imagine if- if you tried to like write, well, you you're shaking your head almost like it’s-
turns.zh: 顺便说一句，我一直很喜欢你的格式，你在很多方面都像个策展人。你有很多经验和好点子，但你并不试图回答所有问题，而是真正邀请领域专家的加入，寻找答案或灵感。我一直很喜欢这种格式，原因有两个：一是它能带来更好的结果、更优质的内容、更贴切的答案；二是它可能更简单。想象一下，如果你试图自己写作，你几乎会摇头——

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Like if I had the answers, I'd be like, “Oh, here you go. I'm done.” You know, the research takes a lot of work and time, but- but I do agree. It ends up being a lot more useful and, and- and valuable. And the reason I did that, just to kind of explain that briefly, is when I left Airbnb, people kept coming to me and asking me like, “Hey, how did Airbnb do this thing? How'd they do that thing.” And I was just like- like, they, they don't know what they're doing. They just did this thing, and who knows if that was the thing that helped them, or if that was the right way of approaching it. So I wanted to do this, like, “What does everyone do? And what seems to be the pattern of the things that work?” And that kind of led to this approach. And it takes a lot of time. Especially this new series that we're gonna chat a bit about that I worked on where it's just like endless interviews and chats and researchers and watching interviews. But yeah, it works out.
turns.zh: 如果我有答案，我会说：“哦，给你。搞定了。” 但研究需要大量工作和时间，不过——不过我同意。最终它更有用、更有价值。我这么做的原因，简单来说，是离开Airbnb后，人们不断来问我：“嘿，Airbnb是怎么做到这个的？他们怎么做到那个的？” 我当时就想——他们，他们根本不知道自己在做什么。他们只是做了这些事，但谁知道这是否真的帮助了他们，或者这是否是正确的方法呢？所以我想做这件事，比如，“大家都怎么做？哪些方法似乎有效？” 这就促成了这种方法。它耗费了大量时间。特别是我们要聊聊的新系列，我投入了大量精力，做了无数采访、聊天、研究和观看访谈。但确实很值得。

turns.speaker: Ryan
turns.en: Yeah, yeah. You- you, how many hours actually, do you put into like a typical essay?
turns.zh: 是啊，是啊。你——你，通常一篇典型的文章要投入多少小时？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Oh, a reverse question. Uh, I would say the-
turns.zh: 哦，换个问题。嗯，我会说——

turns.speaker: Ryan
turns.en: Yeah, I don’t know if I'm supposed to ask you questions, [laughs] but I'm curious.
turns.zh: 是啊，我不知道我该不该问你问题[笑]，不过我很好奇。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: This is banned. [laughs] No, it's cool. I say- I'd say the, uh, median post is about 10 hours. It's like, maybe I kind of work on it through the week. So maybe, like a few days through the week, but the most epic posts take hundreds and hundreds of hours that I kind of work on behind the scenes as I work on the weekly posts. So there's a wide range. Some posts take like three hours and sometimes those do very well, much better than expected.
turns.zh: 这是不允许的。[笑]不过没关系。我会说——我觉得，嗯，平均一篇帖子大概需要10个小时。可能我会在一周内陆续完成。所以一周里可能分几天完成，但最耗时的帖子要花好几百个小时，我会在处理每周帖子时顺便完善它们。所以时间跨度很大。有些帖子只需要三个小时，但有时效果反而特别好，比预期好得多。

turns.speaker: Ryan
turns.en: Yeah. Yeah. I- that's exactly going back to my, my point about like- it takes a long time to write content that you're proud of. Um, I’m also just very particular about words, uh, for better or worse. And so I- the first draft actually is maybe like 20 or 30% of the time. And then the rest is refining it and getting feedback and everything else.
turns.zh: 是啊，是啊。我——这正好回到了我的观点，也就是说——要写出令自己自豪的内容确实需要花很长时间。嗯，我对用词也很挑剔，不论是好是坏。所以第一稿实际上可能只占20%或30%的时间。剩下的时间都在润色、收集反馈之类的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's exactly how I find it. The question I wanted to ask is, startups are so freaking hard… they almost always fail. It's always just like, “Oh my God, this is… Why am I doing this to myself?? My general advice to founders is like, don't start a company, unless you just like, can't not start a company because it's so hard. What's your take there? What do you think? What do you advise founders for when they're thinking about, should I start a company? Should I not start a company? Which- how should I approach this?
turns.zh: 我也这么觉得。我想问的问题是，创业太难了……几乎总是失败。总是那种感觉：“天哪，这也太难了……我为什么要这样折磨自己？” 我给创业者的建议是，除非你非得创业不可，否则就别创。特别是当你犹豫不决的时候。你怎么看？你觉得该怎么做？当创业者纠结“要不要创业？”时，你会给他们什么建议？

turns.speaker: Ryan
turns.en: I do- I do spend time, ironically, like. challenging founders sometimes when they're thinking about raising or thinking about an idea to- to not raise. Um, people who are in tech, uh, especially, are certain bubbles [laughs] of tech, that’s the default. It's like, “The first thing I do, I have an idea, now let's go raise money.” And we've gone through some like pretty massive bull cycles where that- that was possible for a lot of people. But it's a huge decision. So with- with Product Hunt, it was a side project in the beginning. It wasn't actually intended to be a startup at all, but in the beginning, you know, it was a newsletter, then it was a website and it was about four to five months before we even incorporated.And we got a lot of traction. So, it was during that time, I was really just thoughtful around, "Should we raise? Do I wanna work on this for many, many years? What's the opportunity? Is this even a venture backable like idea?" Like all those questions were circulating in my mind for a while. And this is also in a time when the market was pretty, was similarly bullish. This is, uh, end of 2013, early 2014. And investors were- were using Product Hunt to reach out to me, and they were sort courting- courting me, and um, kinda doing that whole song and dance to invest, but I- I just wasn't sure if I wanted to. And so, I don't know, I think a lot of the- those decisions, they're very personal and contextual. However, I think it's super important that founders see a line of sight to work on this for ... I think my rule of thumb is a decade, just do you see yourself working on this for a decade? And maybe it's not a decade that you actually work on it. It probably won’t, it either, it'll probably fail before then as most startups do, but I think it's a good litmus test for yourself to be like, “Do I actually care about this enough? Am I, am I really stoked to work on this for many, many years?” But then, you know, the other thing is, I think a lot of people also think “I need to start a company. I need to start a startup.” And they skip to that step without just tinkering and building and, you know, Product Hunt, we called it, not even a side project, we called it an experiment. And that framing I think, is for me, has always been helpful because it's an experiment is really not about success. Of course you want it to be successful, but the goal is not success. I put that in quotes, it's really to learn and, you know, see if people want this thing and then kind of adapt. And so like an experimental mindset is helpful and I think a valuable way to start. It even goes back to like, why I named the fund Weekend Fund. It's like, what are you tinkering with on the weekends? You know? And how can you be more curious and experimental and kind of your exploration of new startup ideas?
turns.zh:
是的，我确实会——说实话，有时会挑战那些正在考虑融资或打消融资念头的创始人。嗯，尤其是在科技领域的人们，他们身处科技的某个泡沫圈子（笑），这几乎成了默认的思维模式。比如，“我一有想法，就马上去融资。” 我们经历过几次大牛市，很多人在那时确实能轻松融资。但这毕竟是个重大决定。所以对于Product Hunt，最初它只是个副业项目。根本没打算把它当作创业公司，但最初阶段，它只是个新闻通讯，后来发展成网站，而在注册公司前四五个月，我们才获得了大量关注。

那段时间，我一直在思考：“我们该融资吗？我真的想为这件事投入多年精力吗？机会在哪里？这是否值得风险投资？”这些问题在我脑海中盘旋许久。当时市场也正处于牛市阶段——2013年底到2014年初。投资者们通过Product Hunt联系我，试图投资，但我不确定是否要接受。这些决策往往非常个人化且受环境影响。不过，我认为创始人必须能清晰看到未来十年发展路径很重要。我的经验法则是：你能否预见自己在这件事上坚持十年？当然实际坚持时间未必十年，但大多数创业公司确实会失败。所以这是一个自我检验的试金石：你是否真心在乎？你是否愿意为此投入多年热情？

还有，很多人一心想“我要创办公司，创办初创企业”，却跳过磨合阶段直接行动。我们把Product Hunt称为实验项目，而非副业项目。这种定位对我很有帮助，因为实验的核心不在于成功。当然你希望成功，但目标不是成功本身。我用引号强调这一点——关键在于学习，观察市场反应，然后调整方向。实验思维模式很重要，也是宝贵的起点。这甚至解释了为什么我把基金命名为Weekend Fund（周末基金）。周末你在鼓捣什么？保持好奇心和实验精神，不断探索新创意。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I didn't know that's why it was called the Weekend Fund. I thought it's because you worked on it on the weekends, or is it both?
turns.zh: 我不知道这就是为什么叫Weekend Fund。我以为是因为你周末做这个项目，还是两者兼有？

turns.speaker: Ryan
turns.en: [laughs] It had like multiple meetings. Yeah, it was- three meanings: One was- was that I started Weekend Fund when I was building Product Hunt. So it took a lot of pitch- pitches and calls with founders on the weekends. Two, I think a lot of great ideas start by like metaphorically speaking, nights and weekends, um, kind of side projects or ideation. And then the third reason was it was like more friendly. I don't know, I didn't wanna name it. Hoover capital or something like sterile, wanted it to be -
turns.zh: [笑] 那得开好多次会。是啊，有三个原因：第一，当年我在开发Product Hunt的时候创立了Weekend Fund。所以周末得跟创始人们开很多次会、做多次路演。第二，我觉得很多好点子都是在深夜或周末诞生的，比如副业项目或创意构思。第三个原因是这样做更轻松自在。我也不知道，我不想给它起个像Hoover Capital这样冷冰冰的名字，想要更亲切一点。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Wait, that's an awesome name. Hoover capital. Wow.
turns.zh: 等等，那名字太棒了。Hoover Capital。哇。

turns.speaker: Ryan
turns.en: …Capital. Uh I don't know. I, I feel well.
turns.zh: ……Capital。嗯，我也不知道。我感觉挺好的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, it's not on brand,
turns.zh: 是啊，这名字太没特色了。

turns.speaker: Ryan
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是啊。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: But it’s powerful-
turns.zh: 但它很有力量——

turns.speaker: Ryan
turns.en: Um, yeah. [laughs]
turns.zh: 嗯，是啊[笑]。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: As you know, I asked people on Twitter what questions they would want to ask you. And so I'm gonna inter splice these questions as we go through this. And, you just touched on Product Hunt and fundraising, and I'm curious if you were to go back and- and do it again. Would you raise money for Product Hunt, or would you not?
turns.zh: 如你所知，我在推特上问过大家想问你什么问题。所以接下来我会把这些问题穿插进对话中。你刚刚提到了Product Hunt和融资，我很好奇如果让你重来一次，你会不会为Product Hunt融资，还是不会？

turns.speaker: Ryan
turns.en: Great question. So at the time, this is also the thing I ask [laughs] founders is why do you need to raise money? Like, what is it for? Surprisingly, some people like- I don't know, like they don't have a clear answer. For me, It was pretty obvious. Like we needed- we needed to hire, we needed people. Like, I- I didn't have personal capital to- to pay people. There was an alternative, uh, reality where we actually built an open source. I was thinking like, “Is that possible?” Like we're building something for the tech community. I'm sure a lot of people would love to work on this. Could we build it in an open source way, but that like- that's really hard to do. And when you're building a company, you probably don't want to innovate on too many things, um, including like essentially how to build a product and build a team. Anyway, to answer your question, if I- I don't, I don't know what the right at the time raising money was the right decision because I- I wanted to hire and I didn't have personal capital. There really weren't any other realistic options. I don't think. Today I could get further with my own- I'm not super wealthy and I'm super illiquid, but I have at least enough money where I could have funded, you know, maybe a year of development with this very small team. So today it might be a little bit different in which I might not raise venture capital because Product Hunt isn't the type of company that needs to raise a ton of money. It's also one which is not, um, doesn't have like direct competitors in the sense of like an Uber and Lyft situation where raising is actually like kind of mandatory and you sort of have to build a massive war chest to compete. So there- there is a scenario where if I had more money, then maybe I wouldn't have raised venture capital. But yeah… there- there's a lot of other like decisions and other things that probably, uh, bigger mistakes I think I made. Um, not that raising money was a mistake by any means. It was, I think the right decision then, but yeah- there's a lot of learnings in hindsight's 2020.
turns.zh: 好问题。所以当时，我也会问（笑）创始人，为什么需要融资？是为了什么？令人惊讶的是，有些人——我不知道，他们没有明确的答案。对我来说，这很明显。比如我们需要雇人，需要团队成员。但我个人没有资金支付员工薪资。当时还有个替代方案，就是开源开发。我当时想：“这可行吗？”毕竟我们是在为科技社区打造产品。我相信很多人愿意参与。但开源模式实在太难了。而创业公司通常不宜在太多事情上创新，包括产品开发和团队组建。所以回答你的问题，如果我再来一次，我不确定当时融资是否正确，因为我确实需要雇人，而个人资金不足。当时没有其他现实可行的选择。我觉得今天我可以用自己的资金维持，比如虽然我不算特别富有，流动性也不高，但至少有足够资金支持小团队一年的开发。所以今天的情况可能不同，我可能不会融资了。毕竟Product Hunt不需要大量资金，也没有像Uber和Lyft那样的直接竞争对手——它们必须筹集巨额资金才能竞争。所以在某些情况下，如果我有更多资金，可能就不会融资了。不过……确实有很多其他决策和失误，比如我觉得融资本身不是错误。当时这是正确的选择，但回头看确实有很多可以改进的地方。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: The point you made about like, you just needed money to like run the thing. I think that's so, so overlooked when people bash the idea of fundraising for a startup that maybe didn't need it. Like you just need money. Like you don't have just money to burn and go into debt. That makes sense to raise some money and see where this thing goes without really knowing where it's gonna go.
turns.zh: 你之前提到的观点是，创业公司可能不需要融资，但你确实需要钱来维持运营。我觉得当人们批评创业公司不必要融资的想法时，这一点被严重忽视了。毕竟你就是需要钱，又不是有钱可以挥霍、去背负债务。筹集一些资金，观察项目的发展方向再做打算，这样才合理——毕竟你根本不知道项目会走向何方。

turns.speaker: Ryan
turns.en: Mm-hmm .Yeah, especially if it’s… I mean, I think it's very important to raise- raise from people who are aligned with you too. Meaning like, “Why does this person want to, whether it's an angel or a fund, invest in your fund?” Um, sorry, not fund… your company. When you go down a certain path, when you raise a series A, B, C, like you have different expectations and when you raise your proceed or seed round. So I think also understanding like, you know, what you're signing up for is super important.
turns.zh: 嗯，是啊。如果是……我是说，从与你理念一致的人那里融资非常重要。这意味着，比如，“为什么这个天使投资人或基金要投资你的公司？”当你走上某条路径时，比如A轮、B轮、C轮融资，或者种子轮融资，人们对你的期望是不同的。所以我觉得理解自己在签署什么协议非常重要。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What kind of treadmill you’re- you're getting on.
turns.zh: 就像你踏上了一台永动机。

turns.speaker: Ryan
turns.en: Yes. Yeah. ‘Cause you can't get off. I mean you can, but it's not like a company… I always say like when you're at a company, you can put in two weeks, notice one month notice. You can move on. As- as a founder or CEO, you can’t. Like, you really can't. Um, now you technically can… But you can’t, it- it's really, hard, um, to, to exit.
turns.zh: 是的。因为你无法退出。我的意思是，你可以，但公司不一样……我总是说，当你在公司工作时，你可以提前两周通知，提前一个月离职。然后就可以离开了。但作为创始人或CEO，你做不到。嗯，理论上你可以……但实际上很难退出。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. I look at the Airbnb founders. Who've been doing this for 15 years. Like, you know, they're doing well in life, but they also… it's very hard to leave.
turns.zh: 是啊。我看Airbnb的创始人，他们已经做了15年了。虽然他们生活不错，但离开公司也非常困难。

turns.speaker: Ryan
turns.en: Mm-hmm.
turns.zh: 嗯。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. Coming back to Product Hunt, people launch their product on Product Hunt, that's the thing, and I'm curious; founders are always so obsessed with launching and the power of a launch, and "We gotta launch.” Do you think launches are worth it for a company? Is that something founders should be spending time on or is it often better just to not even spend time on that and just build slowly?
turns.zh: 是的。回到Product Hunt这个话题，人们在Product Hunt上发布产品，我很好奇，创始人们总是痴迷于产品发布和发布带来的影响力，总说“我们必须发布”。你觉得产品发布对公司来说真的值得吗？创始人是否应该把时间花在发布上？或者说，不如慢慢积累，慢慢发展？

turns.speaker: Ryan
turns.en: Yeah, I- I always kinda ... Whenever I share like my perspective on stuff, I- I always enforce it always like it kinda depends, which is kinda like it sounds like a cop-out answer. So, it's- it's more ... My answers are usually more nuanced, and the thing about launching is- is going back to why are you raising money. What's the goal? Same thing. Why are you launching? And the the- a lot of people default to things like customer acquisition, "Oh, I wanna acquire customers." But sometimes that's actually not- it's not useful. Launch sometimes doesn't help with that, but there are many other reasons why you might wanna launch. So, customer acquisition one, to get the word out. Another can be recruiting. So, by, you know, sharing your story, getting people excited, it might make it easier to recruit and get people excited about, you know, what you're building. Another is fundraising. Sometimes it can create momentum, you know, as- as other investors, they do read the news and they know that, you know, when this company is more public, they're might be more heat around it- a particular deal. Feedback is one. Um, the feedback from users, feedback just serendipitously and- and sort of another one is partnership. So, as you launch, you might also encounter more partnerships, more opportunities. I think there's a serendipitous effect of launching. So, I think understanding like what are the priorities of the business. Like if you- it might not be customer acquisition at all, it might be, "We need to recruit and hire. Let's launch, so we can get the word out. Hopefully that will help land, you know, our next, you know, engineers, designers, or whoever." And then I also see there's like these little ti- side benefits too of launching that we see a lot through Product Hunt. One of them is team morale. And this- this might- I think this is overlooked. And I- I would also encourage [laughs] founders not to get their team too, um, I would say- you- you shouldn't be motivated to launch a product just to get like the likes on Twitter and the upvotes on Product Hunt, but there is a gr- like a powerful team morale and kinda building moment there where you can all celebrate what you've accomplished and what you built and put it out to the world. And, you know, somebody on the team can share, you know, the- the- the Product Hunt launch or, you know, some Tech Crunch article with their- their mom. And, you know, like that seems like a trivial kind of meaningless thing, but it actually matters for a lot of people. And then the other thing is SEO. So, if SEO's like a part of your strategy, having articles, positive articles, having a- a positive Product Hunt launch, things like that can also be helpful.
turns.zh: 是啊，我——我总是有点……每次我分享自己对某件事的看法时，总会强调这一点，但具体情况得视情况而定。这听起来可能有点推诿。但其实——我的回答通常更细致入微。说到发布产品，关键在于：你为什么要筹集资金？目标是什么？同样，发布产品的初衷是什么？很多人默认的答案是客户获取，比如“我想吸引客户”。但有时这并不可行——发布产品未必能达到这个目的。不过，发布产品还有其他深层意义。比如宣传品牌，通过分享故事激发兴趣，或许能更轻松地招募人才，传递产品理念。再比如融资——有时能制造热度，吸引其他投资者关注。反馈也很重要，用户的反馈可能带来意外收获。还有合作伙伴关系——发布产品后，合作机会可能会增多。发布产品确实能带来意想不到的机遇。关键在于理解企业的优先事项。比如，如果目标不是客户获取，而是“我们需要招募人才”，那么发布产品就能吸引人才，助力团队发展。还有发布带来的团队士气提升，这一点常被忽视。我鼓励创业者不要为了在推特上收获点赞、在Product Hunt上获得投票而发布产品，但发布产品确实能激发团队热情，让大家为共同成果庆祝。比如团队成员可以向亲友分享Product Hunt发布动态或Tech Crunch文章，看似微不足道，但对很多人意义重大。最后是SEO优化——若SEO是策略的一部分，积极的文章和成功的Product Hunt发布能提升排名。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's awesome. I love that last point about morale. I- I hadn't thought about that. You've seen probably more launches than other person out there. How many launches of startups would you estimate you've kind of like seen or been [laughs], I don't know, an observer of? If that makes any sense.
turns.zh: 太棒了。我特别喜欢你提到的团队士气这个点。之前没想过这个问题。你应该见过比别人更多次发布产品吧。我想问你，你估计见过或参与过多少次创业公司的发布活动？如果这说得通的话。

turns.speaker: Ryan
turns.en: Um, I should look at our database on Product Hunt and see how many launches we've had 'cause it's gonna be a subset of that. I mean by seen, I- I- some of it's very high-level, but tens of thousands over the years.
turns.zh: 嗯，我得看看Product Hunt的数据库，看看我们到底支持过多少次发布。说到见过，我指的是高层层面的参与，但这些年累计有好几万次。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay, so when you think about that, do you have any sense of what correlates with a great launch versus just like an okay launch? What- what do founders miss with how they launch?
turns.zh: 好的，那么当你思考这个问题时，你是否有任何感触，知道哪些因素能带来成功的发布，而哪些因素只会导致平庸的发布？创始人在发布过程中容易忽视哪些方面？

turns.speaker: Ryan
turns.en: Yeah, I mean the- this goes back to college and- and the a- you know, I won't go on my own rant about education, but in, uh, you know, English class and writing class, a lot of teachers teach people to write with big words and fill pages of content and basically not speak like a human. And so, one- one thing I've noticed among founders and just people in general is they tend to write like a- a PR person and not like a human and not like, you know, the- the way that I kind of describe kind of a frame of- of writing, maybe your tagline for Product Hunt, um, or for your launch in general is like how- how do your customers or your users describe your product to other people? Or another frame is how do you describe it to your friends? Like when you're just, you know, hanging out, like how do you describe what you do, what you built, what it's for? And that language, I think, resonates with people because it feels way more authentic. And the people that use buzzwords and- and vague language, it just doesn't click. People see right- people are sick of the PR [laughs] speech. And so, I think the language and the microcopy, copyrighting matters so much. And then there's a lot of other things around like we should go more to the product and less about the launch. Like do you really understand who you're building for? And do you understand how to communicate the value prop- like what is it in the mind of user? There's sort of a lot of, I guess, more strategic kinda like decisions that go into that- that, uh, before the launch.
turns.zh: 是的，我的意思是——这要追溯到大学时期，还有——嗯，你知道的，我不会长篇大论地谈论教育，但在，呃，英语课和写作课上，很多老师教导学生用华丽的词汇填满页面，却不符合人类的表达习惯。所以，我注意到创始人以及普通人往往写作时像公关人员而非普通人，更不像——我来举个例子，你的产品标语，或者发布文案，应该怎么写？一种思路是，让客户或用户如何向他人描述你的产品？另一种思路是，你如何向朋友描述？比如，当你们闲聊时，你会如何描述自己的工作、所建产品及其用途？这种语言更能引发共鸣，因为它更真实。而那些用流行词和模糊语言的人，根本无法引起共鸣。人们能看透——他们厌倦了公关式的说辞。所以，我认为语言和微文案、版权保护至关重要。还有很多其他方面，比如我们应该更聚焦产品，而非发布本身。比如，你是否真正了解产品的目标用户？你是否能传达产品的价值主张——在用户心目中它意味着什么？发布前有很多战略性决策需要考虑。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Imagine each of those, uh, points can be its own podcast and block post. [laughs] One of the questions that people asked me on Twitter was the classic, "How do I get to number one on Product Hunt?" So, my question to you is I know that's like ... There's not gonna be a silver bullet. Is there like a guide that you point people to that's like, "Here, just follow this advice," and/or, I don't know, two or three key things that you just gotta get right.
turns.zh: 想象一下，每个要点都可以单独做成播客或推文。[笑]推特上有人问我经典问题：“如何在Product Hunt上登上榜首？”所以我想问你，我知道这类问题……没有万能答案。你有没有推荐的指南，比如“照着这些建议做”之类的，或者两三条关键点必须做好？

turns.speaker: Ryan
turns.en: Yeah. Yeah, so in the posts below, there's actually a link- links to a bunch of guides and FAQs and things like that. So, it's really easy to find like sort of the best practices there. The team also has like this checklist. So, once you launch, there's like a checklist of things, recommendations or tips. And I'm actually forgetting like what each of them are specifically right now, but some of the things that I've noticed that make a big difference is we've already talked about the tagline copy, that goes to, not only the post, but also the maker. Usually people tend to add like some introduction, some context. Uh, generally a lot of people will, they- they manufacture PR speak there too, and so speaking like a human, I think, is important. Also keeping it a little brief. Some people write essays, which might be interesting, but the reality is most consumers, especially people on Product Hunt, you know, they're- they're flipping through a bunch of ideas. They're looking for things that spark their curiosity and interest. And they probably not particularly interested in reading like an [laughs] essay, you know, from- from the makers. So, keeping that short, I think, is helpful. And then another big one is the gallery is- is often the first thing that someone is gonna see once they land on the page. And so, just naturally our eyes gravitate towards visuals. And some of the most interesting presentations I've seen is people use the gallery almost like a slideshow, um, like telling a story, where each slide is- is communicating like a different- well, a story of some sort. It could be like, "Here's the before and after with our product," or "Here's the evolution of what this product can do." There's many different ways to approach it, but like a really clean, you know, visually interesting story, um, can also be a great way to like capture people's interest in what you built.
turns.zh: 是啊。在下面的帖子里，实际上有一些链接——指向一系列指南、常见问题解答之类的内容。所以，在那里找到最佳实践其实很简单。团队还提供了一份清单。一旦你上线产品，就会有一个包含建议或提示的清单。我现在暂时忘了具体内容，但我注意到一些能带来显著效果的方面。比如，我们已经讨论过标语文案，这不仅适用于帖子，也适用于创作者。通常人们会添加一些介绍或背景信息，但很多人会用过于正式的公关术语来写文案。所以，我认为用口语化的表达更重要，同时保持简洁。有些人写长篇大论，虽然可能很有趣，但现实是大多数消费者，尤其是Product Hunt上的用户，他们快速浏览大量创意，寻找能激发他们好奇心和兴趣的内容。他们可能对创作者的冗长长文不感兴趣。因此，保持简洁有助于吸引注意力。另外，图库通常是用户访问页面后首先看到的内容。我们的视线自然会被视觉元素吸引。我见过一些最有趣的展示案例，创作者几乎把图库当作幻灯片来使用，讲述故事，每张图片都传递不同的信息，比如“产品前后对比”，或者“产品功能演变”。虽然方法各异，但用简洁有趣的视觉故事来吸引用户兴趣确实是个好办法。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. That was very tactical and helpful. If you were to launch something on Product Hunt yourself, and it wasn't like hunted by Ryan Hoover, do you think you would get to the top?
turns.zh: 太棒了。这些建议非常实用和有帮助。如果你自己在Product Hunt上发布产品，而且没有被Ryan Hoover重点推荐，你觉得能登上榜首吗？

turns.speaker: Ryan
turns.en: [laughs] I- I mean I don't know. It's- it's funny because if you ... We should do some like historical analysis on Product Hunt 'cause I'd be curious to know the actual numbers, but it varies all over the board. So, some people, they ask me, "Hey, like I don't know, is Product Hunt like ... Do B2B companies do well there?" And I'm like, "Yeah, like a lo- m- probably more B2B companies than B2C companies actually," and so you see, you know, seemingly boring companies that tap into something that- that- that people find useful or resonate- resonates with them, um, can go to the top. And then you also see the weird, wacky stuff, you know, the- the silly apps also hit the top. So, I don't know, it really varies. And sometimes it's also driven by like the almost like the zeitgeist, like what do people find interesting right now? Like what's sparking people's interest? Because Product Hunt, on one side, you are potentially attracting people who might be future users and customers, partners, and so on, but it's also just a general kind of like zeitgeist of the early adopter tech community. Like what are they interested in? What do they find compelling in general?
turns.zh: [笑] 我-我不知道。这很有趣，因为如果你... 我们应该对Product Hunt进行一些历史分析，我很想知道具体数据，但情况千差万别。有些人问我：“嘿，我不知道，Product Hunt是不是... B2B公司在那里表现好吗？”我说：“是的，可能B2B公司比B2C公司更多。” 你会看到看似无聊的公司，只要能提供实用或共鸣的东西，就能登上榜首。然后你也会看到那些奇怪、古怪的应用也能登上榜首。所以，我不知道，情况确实各不相同。有时这还受时代潮流的影响，比如人们现在对什么感兴趣？因为Product Hunt一方面能吸引到潜在的未来用户、客户、合作伙伴，但它也是早期科技社区的一种时代潮流。他们对什么感兴趣？他们普遍觉得什么有吸引力？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Got it. Okay, so I have a bunch of questions from Twitter that people [laughs] wanted to ask you. And so, let me ask you a few of those, and they're kind of a little bit all over the place, but we'll see- we'll see where this goes. Jessica Toye, who's a- she's a PM at Angel List, she's actually a friend. We were together at Airbnb. She asked a great question.
turns.zh: 好的，我现在有来自推特的很多问题，大家[笑]想问你。所以，让我来问你几个问题吧，虽然这些问题有点杂，但看看能聊到哪儿。杰西卡·托伊，她是Angel List的项目经理，也是我的朋友。我们在Airbnb共事过。她提了一个很棒的问题。

turns.speaker: Ryan
turns.en: Yeah. Jess- Jess is awesome. She- shout-out to Jess, she's like been super helpful on the Angel List side, so she's awesome.
turns.zh: 是啊。她太棒了。我要特别感谢杰西卡，她在Angel List方面帮了大忙，真是位好帮手。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Amazing. Okay, she's the best. She asked what you learned as a PM that has helped you in your venture career.
turns.zh: 太棒了。她是最棒的。她问，作为项目经理，你学到了哪些对创业生涯有帮助的经验。

turns.speaker: Ryan
turns.en: Yeah, um, yeah, so my- my background is, uh, marketing and then product management. Pretty quickly, uh, used to work in the gaming industry, which is like, I think, an- an awesome industry. Really hard to make it in that industry, but like amazing place to learn, and no, no, uh, I have so many biases, so I have to like be cautious of that, but I- I- having a product background, I think, is one of the most important aspects of early stage startup investing, meaning oftentimes, when you're building a new company, there are a lot of risks and there's a lot of important things to- to nail, but it all ultimately comes down to the product that you're building. And so, I think having a product management or a product background is helpful. And one, having more, I guess, perspective in evaluating different ideas and- and arguably more important, uh, how the founder thinks about things. So, it might be less about me evaluating the- the- the market need for this particular idea, but it's what's the thought process and how did this founder come to these product ideas and these insights. And so, I think having a product management background is helpful for that, and I don't know, I also just find it really fun to jam on product with founders. And when it's early, early days, there- there's more opportunity to create some sort of impact or, you know, help shape the product in- in a slight way.[00:31:20] Lenny: Awesome. Basically if you're a PM, you've got a lot of the skills that you need to be a founder.
turns.zh:
嗯，嗯，我之前的背景是市场营销和产品管理。很快，我转到了游戏行业。我觉得游戏行业很棒，但要在那里成功很难。不过那是个学习的好地方。不，我有很多偏见，所以得小心些。不过我觉得，有产品管理背景对早期创业投资很重要。意思是，当你创办新公司时，面临很多风险和关键挑战，但最终都归结于你打造的产品。所以，我认为有产品管理或产品背景很有帮助。还有，我觉得在评估不同想法时能有更多视角，更重要的是，了解创始人如何思考问题。可能不是我去评估某个特定想法的市场需求，而是观察创始人是如何思考产品创意和洞察的。所以，有产品管理背景对此很有帮助。我也不得不说，和创始人一起深入探讨产品真的很有趣。在早期阶段，有更多机会创造影响，或者微调产品方向。
[00:31:20] 莱尼：太棒了。基本上如果你是项目经理，你就具备了成为创始人所需的大部分技能。

turns.speaker: Ryan
turns.en: Founder and- and arguably, investor, um, as well.
turns.zh: 创始人，嗯，可能还有投资者。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Oh, and that's right. Okay. So, uh, Leo of Sousa Ventures, who's also an awesome dude, uh, he asked if you could go back and-
turns.zh: 哦，对。好的。那么，嗯，Sousa Ventures的利奥，也是个很棒的家伙，他问如果你能回到过去，再次创建Product Hunt，你会做哪些不同的事？我们聊过这个，但还有其他问题吗？

turns.speaker: Ryan
turns.en: I saw Leo in, uh, Miami, uh, not long ago.
turns.zh: 我不久前在迈阿密见过利奥。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Oh yeah. He moved to Miami too. Oh my God. Everyone's over there. Okay, so [laughs], uh, he asked if you could go back and build Product Hunt again, what would you do differently? We talked a bit about this, but anything else?
turns.zh: 哦，是啊。他也搬到迈阿密了。天哪。大家都去那儿了。好吧，所以[笑]，嗯，他问如果你能回到过去再建Product Hunt，你会做哪些不同的事？我们聊过这个，但还有其他问题吗？

turns.speaker: Ryan
turns.en: Yeah. Um, I've been thinking a lot about this actually lately. And, um, yeah, I mean there's a few things. Uh, one, Product Hunt, in the very beginning, and still today, is very much focused on tech, and there was, at one point, ambition to expand beyond tech into all different types of, you know, categories of products. So, you know, we experimented with podcasts actually, podcast discovery. We experimented in video game discovery, we experimented with book discovery, and the thesis there was, "Okay, this could be actually discovery platform for all of these communities to discover all these different products," and I think there was a lot of good ideas in that. However, I severely underestimated how difficult it would be to do two things: one, the product experience on Product Hunt is very different than how you would wanna discover video games or maybe, in the future, fashion and a bunch of other types of products out there. And two, it's really difficult to translate a community and expand into other communities. Like some- some have done it. Like Reddit is maybe a great example, where Reddit has this massive [laughs] long tail of, you know, every kinda community you can imagine, but very few companies and platforms can actually do that. So, that's one- one regret is we should not have tried to expand horizontally. We should've just focused entirely vertically and- and served the tech community, you know, better and- and with more things, which is effectively what we're doing now. Another regret, another thing I would've changed is I would've- I would've actually tried to monetize and generated revenue sooner. We- we raised a seed in a series A and we had capital to grow, and we didn't actually try to make money until after we required Angel List. And my thinking at the time was, and to some extent, there's some truth to this, is like everything you prioritize is at the cost of something else. You know, you- you're essentially taking focus from one thing and directing it to something else. And what mattered most was growth and to grow the community, but what I really should've done is dedicated maybe 10% of our focus on revenue generation because, you know, it was- once we started generating revenue, we- we did so very quickly, and we go to cashflow, break even, I wanna say a year, maybe 12 months after we started generating revenue. So, if we would've started in 2014 to make some money, we coulda been cashflow, break even, you know, maybe 2015, 2016, which would've just given us a lot of flexibility in kind of owning your own destiny and proving out some of the business model itself. And then like the last thing, uh, I've been thinking about this lately is- is delegation is- is a classic founder challenge. You know, I- I'm just generally a controlling person. That's something I'm working on. And it's really hard sometimes when I have such strong opinions, and I'm very particular about certain things, uh, fully delegate and fully trust everybody. Not necessarily- we have an amazing team. Like I worked with some amazing people, still people that are Product Hunt today like six, seven years later. It wasn't anything about the skills of the team. It was just my own trust and my own delegation, and what I should've done is, you know, up until shortly before I left, I was editing the newsletter every morning, for example, like every morning. I was waking up, you know, 5 a.m., 5:30 a.m., editing the newsletter. I mean that's just kinda silly, you know, to be doing that so many years later after starting.
turns.zh: 是啊。我最近一直在反复思考这个问题。嗯，确实有几件事让我深有感触。首先，Product Hunt从一开始到现在都非常专注于科技领域。曾经我们确实有过野心，想把平台扩展到科技之外的各类产品品类。比如我们尝试过播客发现功能、游戏发现功能、书籍发现功能，但核心理念是——"好吧，这个平台或许能成为所有社区发现各类产品的平台"。我觉得这些想法本身不错，但我严重低估了以下两点挑战：第一，Product Hunt的产品体验与用户希望发现游戏或未来可能的时尚等其他品类存在巨大差异；第二，跨越不同社区并成功扩展其生态极其困难。虽说有些公司做到了（比如Reddit），它拥有海量长尾社区，但真正能实现这一目标的平台少之又少。因此，我最遗憾的两点是：第一，我们不该尝试横向扩张，而是应该全力深耕科技社区；第二，我们本应更早尝试变现。当时我们拿到了种子轮和A轮融资，有充足资金却迟迟未盈利，直到用完Angel List的资金才开始行动。当时我的想法是（某种程度上也有道理），优先级选择必然以牺牲其他事项为代价。你需要把精力从一件事转移到另一件事上。最重要的是增长和社区扩展，但我本该分配10%的精力用于营收生成，因为一旦营收上线，我们就能迅速实现收支平衡。若2014年就开始盈利，我们或许在2015或2016年就能实现收支平衡，从而获得更大的自主决策空间和商业模式验证机会。最后一点，授权问题是创始人面临的经典挑战。我天生控制欲强，这点我正在改进。但当我对某些事物有强烈主见、要求极高时，要完全放权、完全信任他人确实困难。我们的团队很棒，与六七年前加入Product Hunt的优秀成员至今仍保持合作。问题不在于团队能力，而在于我的信任和授权问题。比如直到离职前，我每天早上还在编辑新闻通讯——凌晨5点、5点半就起来处理这件事。多年后回头看，这种做法实在愚蠢。

turns.zh: 嗯，是啊。这确实很艰难。我觉得这种倾向在某种程度上是好的，因为作为创始人，你非常在意产品质量，非常重视自己打造的东西，也非常注重细节。但有时你需要近乎强迫症般的专注。不过，你毕竟无法无所不能地掌控一切。所以，我也不知道，事后回想，我会想：“好吧，我本该多放权给别人的，本该更信任团队。”是啊，总会有更多失误。我自己也经常犯错，但最终结果还是积极的。因为无论如何，你都必须为公司打拼。

turns.zh: 是啊，是啊。有件事……实际上，我最近几周写了一篇博文，但还没法发布，因为内容可能会让别人感到困惑。比如，有些东西我想分享，但又会给别人带来麻烦。所以我不想让别人为难。总有一天我可能会发布这篇文章，但先说点笼统的。Product Hunt确实有过非常艰难的时期，我们作为创始人（甚至不只是创始人，[笑]只是普通人）都经历过不同程度的挑战。哦，是啊，有时候我甚至身体不适，Product Hunt的很多时刻都让我难受。嗯，那真的很艰难。你知道，我也不知道该怎么形容那种感觉——早上醒来时胃里翻腾的焦虑和压力。作为CEO或创始人，某些方面会更困难，因为你还要戴上自信的外表，内外都要保持镇定，让别人信任你。你也不想让他们承受你所感受到的焦虑，不能百分百透明。所以这很艰难，因为我非常重视真诚，也喜欢和真诚的人共事，但作为创始人或CEO，无法把一切都分享出来。总之，每个人在创业路上都经历过困难。积极的一面是，如果……我希望能对正在经历困境的创始人多一些共情。这让我变得更坚强了，也许对某些事情也更豁达了。它只是让我对公司的成长之路有了更深刻的理解。

在商业领域，我一直在思考一个问题——对许多人来说这或许显而易见，但其中也蕴含着微妙之处：势头至关重要。势头具有反馈效应——高势头能催生更多高势头，而低势头则导致低势头恶性循环。公司内部会形成一种能量场，当项目进展顺利、团队士气高涨时，其他人会受到感染，纷纷效仿；反之，若有人拖慢进度、停滞不前，整个团队就会失去动力。所以势头这东西很奇妙，它或许是初创企业最关键的要素之一，当然它也是众多因素的输入端，但把它做好的难度极高。

turns.zh: 是的。这能推广Product Hunt。会很棒的。我们看看（笑）后续发展如何。这取代了我的闪电问答环节，我之前试过的。好的。但实际上在结束前，我还有其他问题想问你们。如果方便的话。主要有两个话题。一个是关于消费类初创公司的，我最近在这方面学到了一些东西；另一个是天使投资。然后就结束了。先从消费类说起。等这篇帖子发布时，我会发布一些我正在做的关于启动和扩大消费类业务的系列内容。我在其中学到了一些东西，想听听你们的看法。一个是，嗯，我们之前聊过，大概99%的消费类应用都做得不好，尤其是那些风投级别的、融资成功的应用。这让我想起消费类业务有多难。最近哪款消费类应用真正火起来了？所以我想听听你们的看法——你们对此怎么看？对于创始人来说，如果要创办一家消费类公司，应该怎么做？

turns.speaker: Ryan
turns.en: Yeah, yeah, it's tough. I mean there's- there's obviously consumer is pretty broad, so there's like different levels of difficulty, I think. Um, the consumer social or gaming, like games, building games, is probably like the- the- the hardest and the one filled with the most failures. And I think a lot of that is because, I think a few things, I think one monetization is generally harder than like a B2B company. Historically, a lot of it's been like advertising driven, and to do that, you have to first get to massive scale for advertisers to really care. And then you have to, you know, double it and double it and double it [laughs] again. So, monetization is super tough, versus a B2B company, it's like people have a problem, they have a need, they are willing to give you money, you know, on day- day one. The other thing about consumer that's tough is you're- you're always fighting different, essentially you're fighting for attention. And so, you might be some consumer social company, but you're- you're kind of like competing with Netflix too, which isn't in your direct domain, but like people could be watching Netflix, or they could be using your product or- or your social app, let's say. So, now you're competing with so many different things. Many of those are incumbents where the consumer also has like built-in habits, routines. Like this is a big- big part about consumers too is eventually you wanna be like an internal trigger in someone's mind where they- they just, without even thinking, they go and use your product or services for some reason. Usually, you don't start that way. You need like external triggers to like pull people in, but eventually you have to get to that point. So, how do you overcome those internal triggers they have for other services, other products? It's really, really hard. And- and then I think a lot of it is, um, like B2B companies, usually you- you have a clear like problem that you're solving. And you could talk to customers, you could understand what are their current behaviors, what- what solutions are they using now, what do they like about them, what do they not like about them whereas, consumer, there's a little bit of that, but it's- it's fuzzier. You know, if you take, um, like Twitter and you kind of even ask someone like, "Why do you use Twitter and like w-" people will have different answers that are all kind of like fuzzy. And they ultimately tend to come down to some sort of like innate human desire. Like it could be, uh, for Twitter, it could be about like, "I wanna be informed with what's happening in the world," or it could be, "I want to feel less lonely or connected to more people," or something like that whereas, if you go to, let's say DocuSign, I think is a great example, of a B2B company, it's like super simple. [laughs] It's like a- a way to get legal docs signed online. That's- that's what it does. It's a thing that people have to do. It's very clear like what it solves. And so, B2B's just like easier to navigate that idea maze. And so, with consumer, you- your- your first blog post on this topic touches a lot on the idea side. And I- I, a lot of it resonated with me, especially the- the insight piece. Like what is- what is the insight that you, as a founder, have to build this thing? Because I think it's really hard to build a consumer company without some sort of unique insight, maybe impossible. And you can get that in many different ways. It could be through your own experiences. I used to write like a problem journal. Like just when things annoyed me or when things were like less efficient, I would write it down as like a note. And I didn't try to solve it. I didn't- didn't say, "Oh, here's the solution." I was just like, "This is annoying." Like, in San Francisco, one example is a lot of people don't have laundry like in their unit. So, I'm like, "That's kind of annoying. Like that's a problem. Maybe there's a solution out there." So, things like that. And I know, there's- there's- there's a bunch of different ways, like, uh, y- your- your blog post does a better summary, I think, of like the different ways different companies like ideated and came up with their ideas, but yeah, many different ways to navigate it but needs an insight of some sort.
turns.zh:
是啊，是啊，这确实很难。我是说，消费者市场非常广泛，所以难度也各不相同。我觉得游戏领域，特别是社交游戏和构建类游戏，可能最难，也最容易失败。主要原因在于，游戏行业的商业化模式通常比B2B公司更困难。传统上，游戏主要靠广告变现，但要想让广告商真正感兴趣，你得先达到足够大的用户规模。然后你还得不断提升用户量（笑）。所以，游戏领域的商业化比B2B公司难得多——B2B公司只要解决用户的问题，用户就会心甘情愿掏钱。  

消费者市场另一个难点在于，你总是在与各种竞争者较量，本质上是在争夺用户注意力。比如，你可能是一家社交游戏公司，但同时还要和Netflix竞争，虽然Netflix不属于你的直接领域，但人们可能会同时使用Netflix和你的产品或社交应用。所以，你要面对诸多竞争对手。其中很多是既有巨头，他们的用户已经养成了固定习惯和使用路径。这意味着你最终要成为用户内心的触发器，让他们无需思考就能自然使用你的产品或服务。通常创业者不会从这个角度入手，而是需要通过外部触发因素吸引用户，但最终必须达成这个目标。那么，如何克服用户对其他服务或产品的固有偏好呢？这真的非常困难。  

B2B公司通常有明确的待解决问题，你可以直接与客户沟通，了解他们的现有行为、使用的解决方案以及优缺点。而消费者市场则更模糊。比如，Twitter很难让用户给出清晰的使用动机，他们的回答往往很模糊，最终归结于人类的某些天生需求。以DocuSign为例，这家B2B公司就简单明了——它就是一个在线签署法律文件的平台，用户必须用到它。这就是其核心价值所在。  

所以，B2B公司更容易破解商业逻辑迷宫。而消费者市场，特别是初创公司，首先需要在理念层面突破障碍。你的博客文章在这方面有很多启发，尤其是关于创始人如何洞察市场需求的部分。我认为，没有独特洞察力很难成功，几乎是不可能的。这种洞察力可以来自多个方面，比如个人经验。我曾经写过“问题日记”，记录那些让我烦恼的事或现象。
效率低下的时候，我会把它记下来，当作一个笔记。但我并没有试图去解决它。我没有——我没有说，“哦，解决方案在这里。”我只是觉得，“这真烦人。”比如在旧金山，很多人住的公寓里没有洗衣设施。所以我就想，“这有点烦人。真是个问题。或许能找到解决办法。”诸如此类的事情。我知道，有很多不同的方法。比如，你的博客文章更全面地总结了不同公司构思和提出创意的不同方式。不过确实，找到解决方案需要某种洞察力。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. I hadn't heard that, u- u- uh, that pr- problem journal idea. I was gonna ask you if you have any suggestions for how to come up with a startup idea, and that's a really interesting one. Is there- yeah, so I guess it'd be cool to hear where that came from and what that led to? Or if there's anything else you found to be useful around that?
turns.zh: 太棒了。我之前没听说过这个……那个，嗯……创业日志的创意。我正想问你有没有什么建议，能帮我构思创业点子呢，这个主意真是太有趣了。你能不能跟我们讲讲这个灵感是怎么来的？又或者你还有其他觉得实用的相关思路？

turns.speaker: Ryan
turns.en: Yeah, yeah, the problem journal is one. And again, like I think it's helpful, not to try to come up with the solution, but just write- just simply write down the problem you- you observed or experienced. Another one I think's interesting is just to like immerse yourself in different communities. Ideally, like maybe like seemingly niche or weird long tail communities. It doesn't have to be that necessarily, but that might be where you'll see more unique insights or- or gather more insights, and you could do that through, I don't know, I'm just thinking subreddits, meeting a lot of people who are like really excited some other thing. It could be like some weird robotics like niche, hobbyist community, for example. And a lot of that, I think, will- will hone or just like create serendipity for ideas. You might see patterns, or you might see, you know, if problem statements emerge from many people in that community that are facing similar things. And then there's like the other- other component too, which is really about like observing trends and- and changes, whether it's like a consumer behavior shift. Let's take an obvious one. Today is like distributed working. So, five- five years ago when the Weekend Fund started, that was one of our themes. It was like I- I- I think distributed working will be on the rise for a number of reasons. One, you know, i- it's harder and harder to recruit. Two, there's a subset of people who really valuable that flexibility and autonomy. And then fast forward, we had COVID, so like we had remote working, and- and now, that's a huge consumer behavior shift. Not just in how people work but also, like going to your Airbnb like world, like Airbnb has shifted their entire product to support more of this remote working kind of lifestyle, just the way that the- the homepage is now more of a catalog of places that you could explore at different times of the year versus Airbnb before was more like, "I have a very specific vacation trip that I wanna take during these days in these areas." It's like a very different like browsing kind of experience. So, that's just one example. Consumer behavior shifts is one thing to observe. The other is technology shifts. So, what- what new thing can you build today that couldn't be built yesterday? And so, there's- there's a bunch of categories around there, like Web3, AI, you know. The biggest shift that we've seen is- is mobile in like early 2010s, um, 'ish, that unlocked a whole- whole bunch of things. So, so, yeah, I think it's observing those shifts and those changes. Last thing I'll say on that is like I think startups, since there are more and more people building companies and technology, there's essentially more efficiency. It's certainly not a- an efficient, super efficient market, but there is more efficiency in problem discovery and- and- and solution exploration. And so, for that reason, you need even more reasons for things to- sort of answers to the, "Why now?" Like what's changed? What insight do you have? Why doesn't this exist already? 'Cause a bunch of people are trying to build something in the space most likely. Just a lot of what we think about, especially on the investing side, when we talk to founders.
turns.zh: 是啊，是啊，问题日志是一个方法。再说一次，我觉得关键不是急于想出解决方案，而是先把你观察到或经历到的问题写下来。另一个我觉得很有趣的方法是，沉浸在不同的社区里。理想情况下，可以选择一些看似小众或奇特的长尾社区。不一定要是那种，但在那里你可能会发现更多独特的见解或收集到更多灵感。你可以通过，比如，我不知道，我只是在想Reddit的子版块，结识很多对其他事物充满热情的人。比如一些奇特的机器人爱好者社区。很多这样的经历，我认为会磨砺你的思维，或者为你创造灵感。你可能会发现一些模式，或者看到许多社区中的人们面临相似问题时出现的共同诉求。然后还有另一个方面，那就是观察趋势和变化，无论是消费者行为的转变。比如，今天提到的远程工作。这是五年前周末基金成立时的主题之一。我认为远程工作会越来越流行，有几个原因。一是招聘越来越难。二是有一部分人非常看重灵活性和自主性。再快进到新冠疫情，远程工作就成为现实。现在，这已经是一个巨大的消费者行为转变。不仅是工作方式的改变，还有像Airbnb这样的平台，他们整个产品都进行了调整，以支持这种远程工作的生活方式。现在主页更多的是不同时间段可以探索的住宿地点，而以前Airbnb更多的是“我要在特定日期去特定地区度假”。这是一种完全不同的浏览体验。这只是一个例子。观察消费者行为的变化是一回事。另一回事是技术变化。比如，今天能做但昨天做不了的事是什么？在技术领域有很多变化，比如Web3、AI等。我们见过的最大变化是2010年代初的移动互联网，它解锁了许多可能性。是的，关键是观察这些变化和趋势。最后我想说的是，创业公司越来越多，越来越多的人在开发产品和技术，效率自然更高了。虽然这肯定不是一个高效、超级高效的市场，但在问题发现和解决方案探索方面确实更高效了。因此，你需要更多的理由来解释“为什么现在是时候？”比如有什么变化？你有什么洞察？为什么这项技术还没有出现？因为很可能已经有很多人在同一个领域尝试了。这就是我们在投资方面常思考的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Wow. There's s- way too much good advice there. Have you written this down anywhere? Is there a Tweet thread people can find like your kind of approach to coming up with an idea?
turns.zh: 哇。这里有太多好的建议了。你有没有把这些记下来？有没有推特话题可以让人们找到你的方法？

turns.speaker: Ryan
turns.en: I have not, I don't think so.
turns.zh: 我没有，我想应该没有。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Cool. All right. Now we have to-
turns.zh: 不错。好的，现在我们得——

turns.speaker: Ryan
turns.en: Blog post for the future.
turns.zh: 写一篇未来的博客文章。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. Or this is the, uh, this is the- the- the content for people to save and use. Thanks for sharing all that. That was really helpful. One other question I wanted to ask you along these lines is around the target audience and, uh, something ... A- an insight that we both share is that it's really important to get really narrow, whatever you focus on initially, as a start up, and it's, for founders, it's often so counterintuitive, they're like, you know, it's like, "Oh my god, why should I focus on the 1000 people? Or 10000 type people- ... Versus the millions that might wanna use this thing?" What's your sense, and where have you kind of seen that become important? Just the idea of getting very narrow of how you're going after.
turns.zh: 是啊。这是，呃，这是——这是供人们保存和使用的内容。感谢你分享这么多内容。这真的很有帮助。我还想顺便问你一个关于目标受众的问题，以及……我们都认同的一点是，创业公司一开始就把目标锁定得越具体越重要，对创始人来说，这往往违背直觉，他们会想，"天啊，为什么要专注于 1000 人？或者 10000 人……而不是可能想用这个产品的数百万人？"你怎么看？在你看来，什么时候专注变得重要起来？就是要非常明确你的定位。

turns.speaker: Ryan
turns.en: Yeah, it's, effectively, the more narrow you're- you're generally, and this is where I throw in the big asterisks, like not for everything, there's always contextual differences, but generally, the easier it is to build a great solution for those people, because now you can actually hone in the product experience, the messaging, and everything to serve exactly those people. And it can help with the product side, it can help with the marketing and go-to market where you- you're messaging ... When people land on your homepage, you don't need to create kind of a broader kind of like value prop to everybody, but really, you can focus on like what is the- the problem this particular audience or community is- is facing. And so, generally, it's just easier. Now there is always that challenge of like, "Well, is this too small? Is it too- too much of a niche if- if my goal is to build like a massive company?" My bias is not to worry too much about that because what you probably find is, over time, opportunities to expand beyond that. You'll see parallels, maybe to other communities or to other problems. And a lot of companies, you know, eventually expand well beyond that. Like I'll go back to Airbnb, you know the story way better than I do, but you know, initially, it was just like, you know, basically couches and extra rooms in houses. And like a lot of people, most people in the US would not do that. Like my parents, not- not in a million years. Even me, like I don't wanna like stay in some stranger's like room. I want my own space, my own house. So, that- that probably at the time seemed really niche and like small, but obviously, they extended- extended well beyond that. Now- now I view Airbnb as like housing in generally speaking. Like their- their TM is housing in- in my mind, which they haven't yet exp- expanded into like real estate sales or like longterm rentals, per se, but like that- that's a possibility.
turns.zh: 是啊，说白了，定位越具体越好——当然不是所有情况都适用，具体情况得具体分析，但总的来说，针对这些用户打造出色的解决方案会更容易，因为你可以优化产品体验、信息传达等各个方面，精准服务这些用户。这对产品开发、市场推广和市场拓展都有帮助，比如当用户访问你的主页时，你无需向所有人推广一个宽泛的价值主张，而是可以专注于这个特定用户群体或社区面临的具体问题。总之，专注更容易。当然，总会面临这样的挑战："嗯，目标太小了？如果我的目标是打造一家大型公司，这样太小众了吧？"我的观点是别太担心。随着时间推移，你会发现有很多机会拓展业务。比如你会发现与其他社区或其他问题存在共通之处。很多公司最终都实现了跨越。比如 Airbnb，我相信你对它的故事比我更熟悉。最初，它只是提供沙发和空余房间的民宿服务。在美国，大多数人绝不会这么做。比如我的父母，绝对想不到。就连我自己也不想住在陌生人的房间里，我更想拥有自己的空间、自己的房子。所以当时这可能看起来很小众、很局限，但显然他们后来做得很成功。现在我把 Airbnb 看作是提供住宿的平台。他们的商标在我的印象中就是住宿，虽然他们还没拓展到房地产销售或长期租赁领域，但这完全有可能。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: This is a good segue to the last topic I wanted to touch on, investing, which I believe you do full-time. Would you say that it's- your full-time gig now?
turns.zh: 这正好引出我想讨论的最后一个话题——投资，我相信你现在全职做投资了。你会说这是你的全职工作吗？

turns.speaker: Ryan
turns.en: Yeah, yeah, it is. Yeah, I'm spending all my time there, and yeah.
turns.zh: 是的，是的。是的，我所有时间都投入到这份工作中了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Cool. So, from what I can tell, the Weekend Fund is killin' it. I'm not an LP, but it feels like it's kind of this underrated juggernaut that's just doing very well. And so, I wanted to ask you a couple questions along these lines. One is what have you learned about investing, angel investing? Especially what's most surprised you?
turns.zh: 太棒了。所以据我所知，Weekend Fund表现得非常出色。我虽然不是有限合伙人，但感觉它就像一股被低估的巨头，业绩一直很亮眼。接下来我想就此问你几个问题。第一个问题是，你在投资、天使投资方面学到了什么？特别是最让你感到惊讶的方面是什么？

turns.speaker: Ryan
turns.en: I mean I feel like there's a lot ... A lot we've learned. So, there's- there's things on the operational side. Like running a fund, there's a bunch of things that go into it, from LP communications, LP fundraising. There's also like ... Vedika who works with me on the fund side, she, um, she describes it as like hygiene. There's also good hygiene when it comes to running a fund. For example, you know, when you meet a founder, you- you- you should get back to them. [laughs] Like if it's a pass, you should let them know. And then there's a lot of different ways that you can do that. Some people, you know, might just say like "pass," and that's not very encouraging to a founder if they gave you no context, no details. There's also an element of hygiene, which is you always follow up with the person that introduced us to that company. And we just feel it's kinda like that's what we appreciate. Like we like to kinda know what happened, like s- have them close the loop. And so, there's like good hygiene, operational things that we've learned and kinda honed over- over the years. I mean the biggest surprise, the biggest surprise has probably been ... I gotta be careful of how this is interpreted in some ways, but it's ... There are cases when I didn't think the company would make it. I- uh, either the product wasn't working, and you know, many months had passed, and it was very clear that they're- they- well, to me, I thought it was clear that, okay, that this probably isn't gonna work out. In my head I kinda wrote it off. And then that company either pivoted or- or some m- like massive partnership or MMA event came through out of nowhere, and so I- I guess the learning is like never count a portfolio company out until it's over. And, you know, uh, that relies on, of course, backing founders that are very resilient and creative and- and, you know, driven to- to create momentum, you know, out of nothing, but- but that's been surprising to me. And it makes me kind of excited because, you know, we invested in over 110 companies now and it's- it's fun to be able to kinda see behind-the-scenes a little bit how all these things kind of play out, both the good and the bad.
turns.zh:
我觉得我们学到了很多……特别是运营层面的。比如运营一个基金，需要考虑很多方面，包括有限合伙人的沟通、基金募资等。还有像Vedika，她和我一起负责基金业务，她把这称为‘基本功’。运营基金也有一些基本规范。比如，当你见完创始人后，应该及时给他们反馈。（笑）如果是拒绝合作，也应该告知对方原因。还有很多沟通方式。比如有些人可能直接说“不感兴趣”，但如果不给出任何背景信息或细节，这对创始人来说很不友好。另外，和介绍我们认识该公司的中介保持沟通也很重要。我们觉得这很重要，比如想了解项目进展，促成交易。这些都是我们多年来不断磨合的基本功。

最让我惊讶的可能是……我得注意措辞，避免引起误解。比如有些公司我原本认为不会成功。产品没起色，几个月过去了，很明显他们没戏了。在我看来，失败已成定局，就放弃了。结果后来这些公司要么转型，要么突然获得重大合作或MMA活动的支持。所以教训就是，永远不要轻易放弃投资组合中的公司。当然，这取决于我们支持的创始人要足够坚韧、有创造力，能在困境中创造机遇。这让我很兴奋，毕竟我们现在投资了110多家公司，能从幕后看到这些故事的全过程，无论成功还是失败，都很有趣。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's such an inspiring takeaway. Does that change how you invest? Like to me, that's like, "All right, I guess I should just take more bets on founders that are awesome." Although, I find just founder bets, it's like a very expensive hobby/approach because there's so there's so many great founders. How is that informed how you invest seeing that happen?
turns.zh: 这真是很鼓舞人心的启示。这会改变你的投资策略吗？对我来说，就是“好吧，那我就应该多押宝在优秀的创始人身上”。不过我发现押宝创始人成本太高了，因为优秀的创始人实在太多了。看到这些情况后，你会如何调整投资策略？

turns.speaker: Ryan
turns.en: I would say we don't, we don't have like, um, it's again, my cop out it's contextual kind of answer. Like, you know, some people are like, "We are a team first only." Some are, "We're market first." Some are, "We're product first." And we- we look at everything kind of holistically, and I think the evaluation of the product is- is sort of a reflection on the team. So, our- our assessment of the thinking behind the product that they built today and maybe some of the traction is a reflection on like the team's abilities and like the thought processes. So, we try to look at it holistically in, um, I mean, yeah, I mean every investor would say like, "Yeah, we wanna back, you know, resilient founders that are very driven, insightful, and all those things," of course. But it's also sometimes hard to like fully evaluate that, unless you really know that person. So, so, we try to- to- to take as much data around like how the product is working and how they made those decisions leading up to this to- to evaluate the team sort of indirectly.
turns.zh: 我想说我们没有固定的模式，我们没有那种，嗯，这又是我敷衍的回答。就像，有些人会说，“我们首先是团队至上。”有些人会说，“我们以市场为先。”有些人会说，“我们以产品为先。”而我们——我们会全面看待问题。我认为对产品的评估其实在某种程度上是对团队能力和思维方式的映射。所以，我们会全面评估产品背后的设计理念，以及产品目前获得的市场反响，这能折射出团队的能力和思维方式。因此，我们试图从多个维度来评估团队，比如产品表现、决策过程等。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's kinda what I've started to do is I- I try not to invest as a founder bet unless I just know them because it's just so hard otherwise.
turns.zh: 这就是我开始采取的策略——除非我非常了解创始人，否则我不会轻易投资所谓的“创始人赌注”项目，因为这实在太难了。

turns.speaker: Ryan
turns.en: Yeah, yeah, there- there's a few founder bets that- that we've made. One, going back to the consumer social kind of thing, he's somebody I've known for many, many years. One of the most talented like designers, engineers, product builders. And I've just been waiting for him to start a company and- and so, that was- that was one of those, "I'm gonna bet on you because I believe in you. I'm not sure about this first idea, uh, you know, who am I to judge? But I don't know if that's gonna be it," but [laughs] he's probably gonna launch 10 apps, and the 11th is gonna be a massive success. And so, that's sort of the- the way I think about those consumer social founder first bets.
turns.zh: 是的，确实有几个这样的创始人赌注案例。比如在社交消费领域，我认识他很多年了，他是极具天赋的设计师、工程师和产品开发者。我一直在等他创办公司，然后，那就是那种“我赌你一把，因为我信任你。我不确定第一个创意是否可行，但我又凭什么评判呢？但我也不确定是否会成功”，但[笑]他可能会推出10款应用，第11款可能会大获成功。这就是我看待这类社交消费领域创始人赌注项目的思路。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love that. Last question along these lines, for someone that's hoping to get into investing or angel investing in the near future, do you have any advice for folks around that?
turns.zh: 我很喜欢这个思路。最后一个相关问题：对于那些希望在不久的将来涉足投资或天使投资的人，你有什么建议吗？

turns.speaker: Ryan
turns.en: Yeah, actually, I wrote a tweet storm and like converted it to a blog post on this 'cause we've get- gotten a lot of ... You probably as well, get a lot of emails or people saying, "Hey, I'm thinking about raising a fund. Like how should I do that?" or "I wanna get into- to venture. I wanna start investing. Like what advice do you have?" So, yeah, I wrote a blog post on this, and there's many different ways to invest. There's, you know, angel investing is one. So, great thing about that is if you have the capital to angel invest, you can do it today, tomorrow. Like you- there- there's no- no sign-offs required. You have maximum flexibility, but of course, you need to have disposable income. You need to be able to- [laughs] be willing to lose all of it and then hopefully you, you know, you'll ma- you'll be on the other side of that and make some money in 10 years. It takes a long time. There's scouting; that's another option. And there are more and more scout funds probably than ever before right now, in different flavors. Some of them are like dedicated kind of scout programs where you have capital to deploy on your own, some are more like you still need approval, but you send the deals, and you get carry on those deals in many cases. Those have pros and cons too. Like they're easier to start and get into than raising a fund typically for most people, but you also are sort of reliant on that- that program or that fund. Um, you might have less autonomy in what you can invest in and what you can't. And then there's a few others; there's SPVs is- is one angle, which works really well for a lot of people. So, um, for those that maybe don't know and- and listening to this right now, SPVs are essentially like a single vehicle, um, investment into one company. So, you raise money from LPs, from other investors, to invest in this specific company. And there are a few great things about that. Like one, you get deal-by-deal carry, meaning like the- the outcome of that company is- is you get paid when they exit essentially, assuming there's a positive outcome versus a fund, like you have to return the entire fund first. Two, it allows you to also bring in maybe very strategic, helpful people into that particular round for that company, which can actually be a- a strong value add for that founder. The biggest trade-off is it's a lot of work sometimes. You- you have to basically do a fundraiser [laughs] every couple you invest in, and that's super time-consuming for a lot of people. And then the last thing is like r- rai- raising a fund. So, that's the decision that I decided back in 2017 is I wanted to raise a fund. It's a lot more work to raise the capital and- and- and there's a lot more responsibility in managing funds and so on and so forth, but it provided me with the most flexibility and- and a way to deploy many checks into many companies, especially when I didn't and still don't have like a ton of money to angel invest. So, yeah, those are like different options. Like I think my blog post goes into more like pros and cons for each of those things, but the last thing I'll say actually is, let's say, none of those are really an option. You- you- you don't wanna start a fund. You don't have enough relationships to do SPVs. You- for whatever reason, you can't do a scout. You don't have any money to angel invest. One thing you can also do is just like pretend angel invest. [laughs] And that doesn't mean that you're meeting the founder and like writing a check, but you can write memos, or you can like almost create a fantasy portfolio. And this is what Vedika, before she joined- joined me, was doing to some extent. She was writing memos about companies she was excited about. And in some ways, she was like doing the job before getting the job, and anyone can do that today. And that can be helpful too if you're applying or trying to prove your- your- your abilities. You could say, "Hey, here are the memos. Here are the companies that I would have invested in, you know, if I had the opportunity, and, you know, here's my thought process behind that."
turns.zh:
是的，实际上，我写了一篇推特长文，还把它转换成了一篇博客文章，因为我们收到了很多这类提问。比如，你可能也经常收到邮件或有人问：“嘿，我正在考虑筹集资金。应该怎么做？”或者“我想涉足风险投资。想开始投资。你有什么建议？”所以，我写了一篇关于这个的博客文章，投资的方式有很多种。比如天使投资就是其中之一。其优点在于，如果你有资金进行天使投资，今天或明天就可以行动。无需任何审批流程，灵活性极高，但当然你需要有可支配收入。可能还要甘愿承受全部损失，然后希望十年后能有所回报。这需要漫长的时间。还有项目评估，这也是一个不错的选择。目前可能比以往任何时候都有更多的评估基金，形式各异。有些是专门的评估项目，你可以自主部署资金；有些则需要审批，但通常你提交交易后，就能获得交易分成。这也有利弊，比如对大多数人来说，启动和参与比筹集基金更容易，但你会依赖于该项目或基金，投资自主权较低。  

还有其他选择，比如SPV结构，对很多人很有效。SPV本质上是针对单个公司的投资工具。你从有限合伙人（LP）和其他投资者那里筹集资金，专门投资某家公司。优点包括：1. 交易级别的分成，即公司退出时获得收益（前提是成功退出），而传统基金需要先退还全部资金。2. 可以为特定轮次引入战略合作伙伴，为创始人创造巨大价值。缺点是工作量大，比如每投资一家公司就得重新筹集资金，这对很多人来说很耗时。  

最后，是筹集基金。这是我2017年决定的选择。筹集资金需要大量工作，管理基金责任重大，好处是灵活性极高，能为多家公司投资，尤其是在我没有大量天使投资资金的情况下。但要实现这些，需要耐心和资源积累。
以下是维迪卡（Vedika）加入我们团队之前所做的一些事情。她会写一些关于自己感兴趣公司的备忘录。从某种角度来说，她是在入职前就提前完成了这项工作。如今任何人都能做到这一点。如果你正在求职或试图证明自己的能力，这会很有帮助。你可以说：“嘿，这些是我的备忘录。这些是我如果有机会的话会投资的公司，还有，我当时的思考过程是这样的。”

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love that. I'm curious about the logistics of knowing the prices of all these startups, but anyway, we don't have to get into all of [laughs] that. That's an awesome idea.
